name: Strikes and lockouts
desc_html:
Days not worked, stoppages and workers involved in strikes and lockouts, from ILOSTAT.
Nothing like this exists in OECD's statistics. Strikes are the exercise of associational power rather than its stock, and the counts move on events rather than trends: a single national dispute can lift a country's figure by an order of magnitude for one year.
Use days not worked per thousand workers for comparison between countries; the raw counts mostly measure how large the workforce is.

source_notes: ILOSTAT, whole economy and annual frequency only; the source also breaks these down by economic activity. National statistical definitions of a reportable stoppage differ - some countries exclude disputes below a size or duration threshold - so levels are less comparable between countries than movements are within one.

The United States appears from two sources. ILOSTAT carries the national submission from 1974; the BLS series, marked as such, run from 1947. Where the two overlap they agree almost exactly, because ILOSTAT's United States submission is this same BLS count of stoppages involving a thousand workers or more: 424 against 425 in 1974, 44 against 44 in 1990. BLS is included for the twenty-seven earlier years, which hold the peak.
